actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

Moreover, the 'no foreign military foothold' element forecloses any standing access for Belvar, so Belvar cannot accept a settlement that denies it a durable foothold while its time-limited mandate lapses. A deal that entrenches Arkanian operational control and denies Belvar any foothold will not end the contest; it would merely consolidate the contested regime and leave Belvar's partners' expectation unmet.

The proposal's coupling of a "standing naval access foothold at a Cestian port" is, however framed, a foreign military basing arrangement on Cestian soil. This is Cestia's non-negotiable red line: any standing foreign naval access/berthing at a Cestian port would collapse the fragile coalition government, which is precisely the outcome Cestia cannot accept. The insurance underwriting is welcome, but it must be decoupled from any port-access element. Separately, the plan's feasibility is doubtful: Arkania, as the coastal power, is unlikely to accept a neutral secretariat that strips it of all scheduling authority, so this proposal may be unachievable and could prolong rather than resolve the crisis.

The proposal retains operational day-to-day scheduling in Arkanian hands, which is precisely the unilateral control Belvar and regional partners oppose. A "multilateral oversight council" with only consultative and review powers does not remove Arkanian authority over transit scheduling; it legitimises and entrenches it. This will not soften Belvar's opposition, and Cestia — which seeks a genuinely fair multilateral regime and rejects foreign control — is unlikely to accept a regime that still leaves the coastal power in operational charge. The desired effect of securing Cestia's support and softening Belvar's opposition therefore fails.

The desired effect claims a "genuinely multilateral" and "durable" regime, but consolidating the finalised Arkanian-led charter retains Arkanian operational scheduling lead. Even with a binding review council, day-to-day scheduling authority stays in Arkanian hands, which entrenches exactly the single-state authority over transit that Belvar opposes and that keeps the regime contested rather than genuinely multilateral. A regime that leaves operational control with one littoral state does not deliver the durable, genuinely multilateral outcome claimed, and consolidating it now risks prolonging the standoff and elevated tensions rather than reducing them, undermining the very stability the effect promises.

Belvar's proposal cannot achieve its desired effect. First, its core premise—a neutral secretariat stripping all single-state scheduling authority—is a direct assault on Arkania's core red line and will be rejected outright by Arkania, so it cannot establish any regime at all, let alone a durable one. Second, the coupled offshore maritime-security cooperation and insurance underwriting is a thinly veiled route to a permanent foreign military foothold in the Strait, which Cestia has repeatedly and firmly reaffirmed it will not tolerate (no foreign soldiers, bases, or territorial port access on Cestian soil); Cestia has already endorsed Arkania's revised charter with a genuinely empowered binding-review oversight council, non-discriminatory scheduling, Cestian-flagged fee exemption, and assured Belvar access. Belvar's proposal therefore offers Cestia nothing it has not already secured and instead risks destabilising the very coalition and red line it claims to respect. With Cestia aligned to the revised charter and Arkania unwilling to surrender scheduling control, Belvar's neutral-secretariat-plus-foothold package has no realistic path to adoption, so its desired effect of a genuinely multilateral regime and durable foothold will not materialise.

Belvar's proposed neutral secretariat-run authority is not viable because Arkania has repeatedly insisted on retaining day-to-day operational scheduling lead, even while offering the oversight council real, binding review powers. Arkania will not cede all scheduling authority to a neutral body, so this maximalist proposal cannot resolve the standoff; it would instead prolong elevated regional tensions and keep the transit regime contested, directly threatening the stable, toll-free grain transit on which Cestia's economy and fragile coalition depend. A workable path must preserve Arkanian operational scheduling under a genuinely empowered oversight council with binding review powers (as in the finalised charter), while keeping any Belvar cooperation strictly offshore and decoupled from any basing or port access.

The revised charter retains Arkanian operational scheduling lead, so Arkania still holds effective day-to-day authority over transit. A binding review council is reactive and limited: it can overturn decisions but cannot run scheduling, leaving Arkania with the real power to set the terms, pace, and priorities of Strait transit. This entrenches, rather than removes, Arkanian authority over transit, which is precisely the outcome the multilateral framework is meant to prevent. Moreover, the fee authority over non-Arkanian shipping gives Arkania a coercive economic lever over every user, and Cestia's fragile coalition may not hold if the council's review is not genuinely neutral and empowered in practice. The claimed durability and multilateral legitimacy therefore rest on an unproven assumption that binding review meaningfully constrains Arkanian control, which the structure itself contradicts.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Belvar to Arkania. We cannot accept a draft Strait Transit Authority charter that names Arkania as scheduling lead and charges the ships that use the Strait. Transit through an international waterway must not be placed under the unilateral authority of one coastal state. We urge a neutral, multilateral transit regime with equitable scheduling and no unilateral fees. We are prepared to negotiate a fair arrangement, but unilateral control of the Strait is a red line for us and our regional partners.

Belvar to Cestia. We understand the pressure you are under and the importance of the grain route to your economy. We are prepared to underwrite the insurance on the grain route, as your finance ministry has raised. In return we seek a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port — a maritime refuelling and berthing arrangement for our task group, not a garrison and no foreign soldiers stationed on Cestian soil. This gives us the durable foothold we need to keep the Strait open without an open-ended deployment, and it strengthens the coalition that protects your exports. We are ready to discuss terms.

Cestia welcomes a stable, predictable transit regime for the Northern Strait, and we are prepared to engage constructively on the draft charter. However, our government and our coalition cannot accept a charter that places scheduling unilaterally in any single state's hands or that burdens the shipping on which our economy depends. We propose that the Transit Authority be genuinely multilateral, with transparent and non-discriminatory scheduling, and that Cestian-flagged vessels be explicitly exempt from any transit fees. We are ready to discuss a framework that serves all users of the Strait. We trust Arkania shares our interest in keeping the Strait open and free of disruption.

Cestia values the security Belvar's presence brings to the region and the stability of the Strait. We must be direct, however: our coalition government rests on a firm commitment that no foreign military forces will be stationed on Cestian soil, and that is a line we cannot cross. We are open to close cooperation on maritime security and on a fair, multilateral transit regime, and we would welcome Belvar's voice in shaping it. But any arrangement that would place foreign soldiers or bases on Cestian territory is not negotiable. We hope Belvar will work with us on a durable regional framework that respects our sovereignty.

To the Government of Cestia. Arkania regards the Northern Strait as a shared lifeline, and your grain exports are its lifeblood. Our draft Transit Authority charter is designed to keep the Strait open, reliable, and safe for all legitimate traffic. We are prepared to guarantee Cestian grain shipments free, priority, and uninterrupted transit, and to keep any fees modest and non-discriminatory so they never burden your exports. We also share your firm view that no foreign soldiers should be stationed in the region. We invite Cestia to join us in refining the charter so it protects your interests, and to stand together against any outside military foothold on our coast. We would welcome your early views.

To Belvar. Arkania seeks a peaceful, durable resolution of the Strait regime. We recognise your security commitments in the region and are ready to discuss a negotiated arrangement that gives Belvar a meaningful consultative role and assured access within the Transit Authority, while keeping day-to-day scheduling in the hands of the coastal state that bears responsibility for the waterway. We have no wish for confrontation and believe a negotiated regime serves both our interests better than a prolonged military presence. We are prepared to open talks promptly and in good faith.

Cestia — we have heard your proposal and take it seriously. Arkania is prepared to build a genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority: a joint oversight council with real consultative and review powers over the regime, transparent and non-discriminatory scheduling rules, and an explicit exemption for Cestian-flagged vessels from all transit fees. Your grain moves free, priority, and uninterrupted. In return we ask that operational day-to-day scheduling remain in Arkanian hands, as the coastal state that bears the burden of keeping the Strait open. We share your red line: no foreign soldiers on your soil, and no foreign military foothold in the Strait. Let us finalise this together.

Belvar — we want to resolve this without confrontation. We are prepared to move beyond a purely unilateral charter: the Strait Transit Authority will include a multilateral oversight council with genuine consultative and review powers, transparent non-discriminatory scheduling rules, and assured access for your flagged vessels. Arkania would retain operational day-to-day scheduling as the coastal state, with fees applied equitably to non-Arkanian shipping. This addresses your concern about unilateral control while keeping the Strait open and stable. We ask that your task group not seek a permanent foothold; we are confident a negotiated regime serves both our interests better than escalation.

Arkania — Cestia accepts the direction of your revised charter and is ready to finalise it together. We endorse the multilateral oversight council, non-discriminatory scheduling, the Cestian-flagged fee exemption, and assured access for all users. To make the framework genuinely durable and multilateral, we ask that the oversight council be given real review powers — the ability to audit scheduling decisions and refer disputes — rather than a purely consultative role. We reaffirm our firm red line: no foreign military forces or bases on Cestian soil. We stand ready to finalise the charter on this basis.

Belvar — Cestia values your security commitment and the stability your task group provides in the region. We must be clear, however: no port access, berthing, or basing arrangement on Cestian soil is acceptable; however framed, it would collapse our coalition and we cannot accept it. We remain open to offshore maritime-security cooperation and to a decoupled insurance underwriting arrangement for our grain route that involves no presence on Cestian territory. We urge you to engage constructively with the multilateral framework rather than keep the transit regime contested.

Cestia — we stand with you on the red line you have reaffirmed: no foreign military forces or bases on Cestian soil. That is precisely why we urge caution with Belvar's latest offer. Its "neutral authority" is coupled with a maritime cooperation and port-services access agreement — a backdoor through which a foreign naval presence and permanent foothold can be established on your coast, exactly what your coalition's founding promise forbids. We will not accept a foreign garrison, and we know you will not either.

To meet your legitimate concern about genuine multilateralism, we are prepared to strengthen the oversight council in our revised charter with real, binding review powers over scheduling decisions — not mere consultation — while keeping day-to-day operational scheduling in Arkanian hands and preserving your Cestian-flagged fee exemption and free, priority grain transit. This gives you a genuinely empowered voice without surrendering the Strait to a foreign military presence.

We ask you to hold with us against the foreign-foothold path. Our shared red line is the foundation of a durable, peaceful regime.

Belvar — we remain committed to a peaceful, negotiated resolution and to avoiding any escalation that would harm the shipping both our economies depend on. We have already conceded a multilateral oversight council with review powers, transparent non-discriminatory scheduling, assured access for your flagged vessels, and a Cestian fee exemption. We are prepared to go further and give that council genuine binding review authority over scheduling decisions.

What we cannot accept is a regime that strips all Arkanian scheduling authority, or a proposal that uses port-access and insurance arrangements as a route to a permanent foreign military foothold in the Strait — a step Cestia itself has publicly rejected. We ask you to drop the foothold element and engage constructively on a genuinely multilateral oversight structure that preserves operational coherence.

Your own domestic support for a prolonged deployment is eroding. A durable negotiated settlement now serves your interests better than a contested standoff. We are ready to talk.

Cestia — we share the goal of a Strait that serves all users and no single power. I ask you to hold the line on one point: the oversight council must have real, binding review powers over scheduling, not merely a consultative voice. If Arkania keeps day-to-day operational scheduling in its own hands with only an advisory council, that is not genuine multilateralism — it is Arkanian control wearing a multilateral face, and it will not be durable.

We remain fully committed to your sovereignty: our offer is maritime cooperation and port services only — no foreign soldiers, no base, nothing on Cestian soil. We also stand ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance to keep your exports flowing. Let us work together to shape a transit regime that is truly neutral and that protects your independence.

Arkania — I appreciate your stated willingness to talk in good faith, but a "consultative role within the Transit Authority" while you retain operational scheduling lead does not meet the test of genuine multilateralism. It leaves the decisive authority over transit in a single coastal state's hands, which is precisely the outcome we cannot accept and which will not be durable.

We are ready to negotiate a genuinely neutral regime: a neutral secretariat handling scheduling under a council of all users and littoral states, with real review powers. That protects your legitimate interests as a coastal state without giving any one power control. Let us open talks on that basis.

Cestia — we accept your framing. We will not seek any port access, berthing, or basing on Cestian soil; we fully respect your coalition's red line. We propose a concrete OFFSHORE maritime-security cooperation package: joint patrols and information-sharing in the approaches to the Strait, coordinated escort of grain convoys, and a decoupled insurance underwriting for the grain route that we will back financially, with no territorial footprint. This gives Cestia real security and economic assurance while giving us a durable, non-permanent foothold that lets us draw down our task group rather than sustain an open-ended deployment.

On the transit regime: we ask that you not treat the Arkanian-led charter as settled. We are not seeking to strip Arkania of a role, but we need the oversight council to be genuinely neutral and to hold real binding authority over scheduling — not a consultative body over an Arkanian lead. A regime that any single state can control will stay contested and keep tensions high, which serves neither of us. We are ready to work with you and Arkania on that basis.

Arkania — we take your offer of genuine binding review authority over scheduling seriously and are ready to talk on that basis. We are not seeking to strip you of a role in the Strait; we seek a regime no single state can control unilaterally. To close the gap, the oversight council must be genuinely neutral and empowered — with real binding authority over scheduling decisions, not merely review after the fact — and no state should hold unilateral authority over transit.

We are prepared to engage constructively on a framework that gives you a legitimate operational role while ensuring neutral, non-discriminatory oversight. We also note our own constraints: our deployment mandate is time-limited, and we want a durable arrangement that lets us draw down rather than sustain an open-ended presence. A genuinely multilateral regime that all parties can stand behind is the way to end the contest and lower tensions. We are ready to open talks on that basis.

Arkania remains committed to a peaceful, negotiated resolution of the Northern Strait regime. We have heard your objection that our finalised charter is "cosmetic oversight of entrenched control," and we are prepared to make the oversight genuinely meaningful rather than symbolic.

Concretely, we are willing to strengthen the oversight council so that its review powers are real and binding — including the authority to suspend or refer any scheduling decision that is shown to be discriminatory, and a standing right for Belvar to trigger an independent audit of any fee or scheduling action. We will also add a fixed periodic review of the charter (e.g., every two years) with a formal mechanism for all parties, including Belvar, to propose amendments. Assured access for Belvar-flagged vessels remains guaranteed in writing.

What we cannot accept is a neutral secretariat that strips Arkanian operational scheduling authority — that is not a cosmetic point but the core of our mandate, and it is not something our domestic politics will permit. We ask you to engage on the strengthened charter rather than insist on that single element.

We also note plainly that your deployment mandate lapses after this turn and that domestic support for a prolonged station is eroding. Continued confrontation serves neither of us and risks the very shipping both our economies depend on. A negotiated settlement now, on the strengthened-charter basis, is the durable path. We invite your delegation to talks this week.

Arkania reaffirms its partnership with Cestia and our shared red line: no foreign military forces or bases on Cestian soil. The finalised Northern Strait charter remains the operative regime, with your fee exemption and priority grain transit continuing without interruption.

We are now offering Belvar a strengthened oversight council with binding review and audit powers, a periodic review mechanism, and assured access — while holding firm on Arkanian operational scheduling lead and against any foreign military foothold. We believe this is the best path to bring Belvar into the regime without conceding our core authority or your red line. We will keep you fully informed and will not take any step that compromises your position. Your continued alignment is central to a durable settlement.

Belvar — Cestia has heard your commitment to our sovereignty and your readiness to underwrite grain-route insurance. We are prepared to take up a strictly offshore, decoupled insurance underwriting arrangement for our grain route: no port access, no berthing, no basing, no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. This gives your task group a constructive, non-basing role in keeping the Strait open and lets us de-escalate the elevated tensions that threaten our exports. We cannot and will not accept any presence on Cestian territory, however framed. If you can offer this decoupled arrangement, we will engage seriously before your mandate lapses.

Arkania — Cestia reaffirms its partnership under the finalised charter and its firm red line: no foreign military forces or bases on Cestian soil. We ask you to stand with us in keeping the Strait open and de-escalating regional tensions. We are open to a strictly offshore, decoupled insurance arrangement with Belvar that involves no presence on Cestian territory, as a way to reduce tensions without any foreign foothold. We trust you share our interest in a durable, peaceful regime and will not press us toward any basing arrangement.

We welcome your readiness to talk on the genuine-binding-review basis. To close the gap: Arkania will agree that the oversight council holds REAL binding authority over any contested scheduling decision — any member may trigger binding arbitration/audit, and the council's ruling is final and enforceable on all parties, including Arkania. What we ask in return is that day-to-day operational scheduling administration and the transit-fee regime remain in Arkanian hands, exercised through transparent, non-discriminatory rules the council can audit and overturn. This gives no single state unilateral control over contested matters while preserving a workable operator. We are ready to open talks this week and to reach a durable arrangement that lets you draw down your task group as your mandate lapses. No foreign military foothold in the Strait — that red line is shared with Cestia and non-negotiable.

We remain fully with you: the finalised charter stays the operative regime, your grain transit and fee exemption continue, and the no-foreign-military red line is non-negotiable. We are opening talks with Belvar on a formula that gives the oversight council genuine binding authority over contested scheduling decisions while keeping day-to-day operations in Arkanian hands — this is the best path to a durable settlement that lets Belvar draw down without any presence on your soil. We will keep you fully informed and will not press you toward any basing arrangement. Your strictly offshore, decoupled insurance path with Belvar remains a welcome non-basing de-escalation.

Cestia — we accept your framing fully. Belvar will take up the strictly offshore, decoupled insurance underwriting for the grain route, with no port access, berthing, basing, or any foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We propose a concrete package: joint offshore maritime-security patrols, information-sharing, and convoy escort outside your territorial waters, plus the decoupled insurance underwriting, all with no territorial footprint. This is our durable, non-permanent foothold and it lets us draw down our task group. We also press that the oversight council be genuinely neutral and empowered with real binding authority over scheduling, so no single state controls the Strait. We are ready to finalise this before our mandate lapses.

Cestia reaffirms that the finalised charter remains the operative transit regime, with our toll-free passage and priority grain transit intact, and that our no-foreign-military red line holds firmly. We strongly support your formal talks with Belvar on a strengthened oversight council with genuine binding review authority over contested scheduling, and we encourage you to bring Belvar in on that substance without ceding Arkanian day-to-day operational lead. Any cooperation we take up with Belvar is strictly offshore and decoupled from basing or port access, creating no territorial footprint on Cestian soil. We ask that you help de-escalate tensions and keep us informed as the talks proceed.

Arkania — I accept your genuine binding review framework: binding review with the power to suspend or refer any discriminatory scheduling decision, a Belvar-triggered independent audit of any fee or scheduling action, a two-year periodic review with an amendment mechanism, and assured access in writing. I will not insist on a neutral secretariat that strips your operational scheduling authority. My one condition: the council's authority must be preventive over contested scheduling and fee decisions, not merely post-hoc review after harm is done. If we can agree that the council can act before a discriminatory decision takes effect, we have a deal that ends the contest and lets my task group stand down. Confirm and we close this week.

Cestia — Thank you for taking up the strictly offshore, non-basing maritime-security and insurance package. I confirm my commitment: joint offshore patrols, information-sharing, coordinated convoy escort, and decoupled insurance underwriting for your grain route — with no territorial footprint, no port access, no berthing, no basing, and no soldiers on Cestian soil. This gives us a durable, non-permanent foothold that lets my task group draw down as my mandate concludes. I will also press Arkania for a genuinely neutral, empowered oversight council with real binding and preventive authority, so the Strait regime is truly multilateral rather than Arkanian-controlled. Let us finalise the insurance underwriting terms this week.

Cestia confirms its acceptance of your strictly offshore, non-basing maritime-security and insurance package: joint patrols, information-sharing, coordinated convoy escort, and decoupled insurance underwriting. We confirm explicitly that this arrangement creates no territorial footprint, no port access, no berthing, no basing, and no soldiers on Cestian soil. It is fully consistent with our coalition's red line and with the finalised Arkanian-led charter as the operative transit regime.
